cards.meaning: How a single-threaded JS runtime decides what runs next after the current call stack empties. The host queues callbacks; the loop picks them only when the stack is empty. This unit is the scheduler, not Promise settlement.

Call stack (what is running now — sync, LIFO). Macrotask/task queue (timers, I/O, script turns, many host callbacks). Microtask queue (Promise jobs, queueMicrotask, async/await continuations). Queues run only when the current turn's stack is empty.

cards.front: Can a queued callback start mid-function?
cards.meaning: No. Nothing from the queues starts mid-function unless that function schedules work and later returns — or hits await, which exits the current sync portion and schedules a continuation.

cards.front: When are queues eligible to run?
cards.meaning: Only when the stack for the current turn is empty. A busy stack delays timers, I/O callbacks, Promise reactions, and UI work — even if the host already finished waiting.

cards.front: Is the initial script a macrotask?
cards.meaning: Yes — the whole classic script/module evaluation turn is the initial macrotask. Sync logs and scheduling happen there before any queued callbacks.
No — it is a minimum until the callback is eligible. The callback is still a macrotask; if the loop is busy (stack or microtasks), it runs later than the delay.
cards.notes: Common trap: treating the delay argument as exact.

cards.meaning: promise.then/catch/finally, queueMicrotask(fn), await resume after the awaited value settles, MutationObserver (browser). process.nextTick is Node-only and runs even before ordinary microtasks.

cards.front: Why two queue priorities, not one?
cards.meaning: Microtasks finish related Promise bookkeeping before yielding to timers, UI, or I/O. If reactions waited behind every timer and paint, chains would feel randomly delayed. If everything were a microtask, a busy chain could starve rendering — and that starvation is still possible if you abuse microtasks.

1) Run the current sync script / current macrotask to completion (one at a time). 2) Drain the entire microtask queue — including microtasks scheduled while draining — until empty. 3) Browser: pending rendering/UI if it is time to paint. 4) Pull the next single macrotask. 5) Go back to step 2. That drain-all-microtasks rule resolves most predict-the-output questions.

cards.front: Sync; setTimeout(0); Promise.then chain; sync — order?
cards.meaning: 1, 5, 3, 4, 2. Whole script is the initial macrotask (logs 1, schedules timer, schedules first Promise microtask, logs 5). Then drain all microtasks, including the nested .then (3 then 4). Then the timer macrotask (2). Nested .then still beats the next timer; Promise.then from the same turn always beats setTimeout(0).

cards.front: async f: log f1; await null; log f2 — with sync caller?
cards.meaning: s1, f1, s2, f2. Code before the first await runs synchronously as part of the current turn; the rest is scheduled like a Promise.then (microtask) once the awaited value is settled. await does not block the JS thread — it exits the current sync portion so other JS can run. Continuations beat later setTimeout(0).
cards.example: log s1; f(); log s2 → s1, f1, s2, f2

cards.meaning: Yes — if a microtask keeps scheduling more microtasks, the queue never empties, so the loop never reaches the next macrotask or (in a browser) the next paint. UI looks frozen though timers are scheduled. Prefer bounded work per turn; chunk CPU across macrotasks (setTimeout(0), MessageChannel, rAF) when you need to yield.
cards.example: function flood() { Promise.resolve().then(flood); } flood(); setTimeout(() => console.log('never'), 0);

cards.meaning: One awareness card, not phase trivia: nextTick drains before ordinary Promise microtasks (Node-only). Flooding nextTick starves I/O/timers even harder. setImmediate is a Node check-phase macrotask, not web; timeout vs immediate order can vary — don't memorize it. Don't recite timers/poll/check phases; the load-bearing model is still macrotask vs microtask drain-all. Prefer queueMicrotask/Promises for portable code.

cards.front: Classify setTimeout, setImmediate, then, queueMicrotask, await, nextTick?
cards.meaning: setTimeout/setInterval: macrotask. setImmediate (Node): macrotask (check). promise.then/catch/finally: microtask. queueMicrotask: microtask. await resume: microtask. process.nextTick: before microtasks (Node). I/O callbacks and UI events: macrotasks.
No. Still one stack; they run one after another. Parallel JS is not how the queues work.
Host finishing only enqueues; the event loop decides when JS runs the callback — stack must be empty and scheduling rules satisfied.
